title: From Programming Approaches to Object-Oriented Design

questions.q: What is a programming approach, and why does the choice of approach matter?
questions.a: A programming approach (paradigm) is a way of thinking about and organising a solution. The same problem can be solved using different paradigms. The choice affects readability, maintainability, reuse and scalability. The key question is: how do we organise software as systems become larger?

options: A way of thinking about and organising a solution; the choice affects readability, maintainability, reuse and scalability
A specific programming language syntax; it determines which libraries are available
A set of design patterns that must be applied to every project
The order in which a program's statements are executed at runtime

questions.tip: Answer in two parts: (1) what it is, (2) the four consequences - readability, maintainability, reuse, scalability.

questions.q: Name the five programming approaches and state what each organises around.
questions.a:
1. Procedural - organises around procedures/functions.
2. Object-Oriented - organises around objects + responsibilities.
3. Functional - organises around functions + transformations.
4. Logic - organises around facts, rules and relationships.
5. Event-Driven - organises around events + handlers.

options: Procedural, Object-Oriented, Functional, Logic, Event-Driven
Procedural, Object-Oriented, Functional, Logic, Declarative
Procedural, Structural, Functional, Logic, Event-Driven
Object-Oriented, Functional, Imperative, Logic, Event-Driven

questions.tip: Memorise as P-O-F-L-E. One line each is enough for full marks.

questions.q: Describe procedural programming. Give two advantages and two limitations.
questions.a:
Main focus: what steps should the computer perform? A problem is decomposed into procedures or functions. State/data is often passed between or shared by procedures. It is natural for algorithms and small, well-defined tasks. Languages: Basic, C, Pascal.
Advantages: clear for small step-by-step problems; functions can be tested and reused; often easy for beginners.
Limitations: shared data can become scattered; large systems can create complex dependencies; changes to data structures may affect many functions.

options: Focus: what steps the computer should perform. Limitations: shared data can become scattered, and changes to data structures may affect many functions
Focus: what transformations to apply to data. Limitations: immutable data is hard to model
Focus: what facts and rules are true. Limitations: poor at expressing relationships
Focus: what should happen when an event occurs. Limitations: event chains are hard to trace
mcq.stem: Procedural programming: what is its main focus, and which limitations are listed?

questions.tip: Example to quote: ATM withdrawal = read card, verify PIN, check balance, enter amount, deduct, dispense cash.

questions.q: Describe functional programming and give its advantages and limitations.
questions.a:
Main focus: what transformations should be applied to data? Functions are the primary building blocks; it emphasises immutable data and minimising side effects; functions can be composed into larger operations. Languages: Haskell, F#.
Advantages: good for data processing and transformations; pure functions can be composed.
Limitations: can be less intuitive for entity-rich business domains.

options: Main focus: what transformations should be applied to data; emphasises immutable data and minimising side effects. Languages: Haskell, F#
Main focus: what steps to perform in sequence. Languages: C, Pascal
Main focus: entities and their responsibilities. Languages: C#, Java
Main focus: facts and inference rules. Languages: Prolog

questions.tip: Example to quote: student marks -> calculateTotal() -> calculateAverage() -> calculateGrade() -> Result.

questions.q: Describe logical programming and event-driven programming, with one advantage and one limitation of each.
questions.a:
Logical programming organises around facts, rules and relationships, and supports reasoning and inference. Advantages: expressive for relationships, constraints and rules; natural for expert/rule-based systems. Limitations: less common for general commercial application development; not always natural for systems dominated by changing object state.
Event-driven programming organises around events and handlers; the flow is triggered by events rather than one fixed sequence. Common in GUIs, web applications and games. Limitation: event chains can become difficult to trace.

options: Logic organises around facts, rules and relationships; Event-Driven organises around events and handlers
Logic organises around events and handlers; Event-Driven organises around facts and rules
Logic organises around functions and transformations; Event-Driven organises around procedures
Logic organises around objects; Event-Driven organises around data transformations
mcq.stem: Which pairing of approach to description is correct?

questions.tip: Logic example: Programming 1 is a prerequisite of Programming 2 - can John enrol?

questions.q: Complete the 'key question' for each approach: Procedural, Functional, Logical, Object-Oriented, Event-Driven.
questions.a:
Procedural -> What steps should I perform?
Functional -> What transformation should I apply?
Logical -> What facts and rules are true?
Object-Oriented -> What objects exist and how do they interact?
Event-Driven -> What should happen when an event occurs?

options: Procedural: What steps should I perform? Functional: What transformation should I apply? OO: What objects exist and how do they interact?
Procedural: What objects exist? Functional: What steps should I perform? OO: What transformation should I apply?
Procedural: What facts and rules are true? Functional: What objects exist? OO: What events occur?
Procedural: What should happen when an event occurs? Functional: What steps should I perform? OO: What facts are true?
mcq.stem: Which mapping of approach to key question is correct?

questions.tip: This is a very common short-answer / matching question. Learn verbatim.

questions.q: Choose a primary approach for each scenario and give one reason: (A) a tiny temperature converter, (B) an online banking system with customers, accounts, payments, cards and transactions, (C) a pipeline that resizes, filters and classifies millions of images, (D) a mobile game with player input, collisions, enemies, score and UI events.
questions.a:
A - Procedural: small, sequential, step-by-step algorithmic task with a clear input-process-output flow.
B - Object-Oriented: many real-world entities with state, relationships and responsibilities that must be maintained and extended.
C - Functional: pure data transformations applied in a pipeline; functions compose well and avoid side effects.
D - Event-Driven: the flow is triggered by events (input, collisions, UI) rather than one fixed sequence.

options: Procedural, Object-Oriented, Functional, Event-Driven
Functional, Procedural, Object-Oriented, Event-Driven
Procedural, Event-Driven, Functional, Object-Oriented
Object-Oriented, Functional, Event-Driven, Procedural
mcq.stem: A tiny temperature converter, an online banking system, an image-processing pipeline, and a mobile game driven by player input. Which approach best fits each, in that order?

questions.tip: Always justify with the nature of the problem (scale, entities, data transformation, or events), never just 'because it is modern'.

questions.q: Define Object-Oriented (OO) as used in this course.
questions.a: OO is a software engineering approach to analyse a problem, design a solution, and implement it using software in which the structure is based on objects interacting with each other to accomplish a task.

options: A software engineering approach to analyse a problem, design a solution and implement it using software structured around objects interacting with each other
A programming language feature that lets one class inherit from another
A notation for drawing diagrams of database tables and their relationships
A testing technique that verifies objects in isolation using mocks

questions.tip: Three verbs to remember: analyse, design, implement - and 'objects interacting with each other'.

questions.q: Explain the three phases of Object-Oriented Development.
questions.a:
1. Analysis - developing conceptual models of solving a software problem. (think about the problem)
2. Design - realising the analysis with object-oriented system models that could implement the requirements. (present 'potential' ideas that describe the solution)
3. Programming - realising the object-oriented design by using an object-oriented programming language such as C#, Java or Python. (solve the problem with software)

options: Analysis (conceptual models, thinking about the problem), then Design (OO system models implementing the requirements), then Programming (realising the design in an OO language)
Design, then Analysis, then Programming
Programming, then Analysis, then Design
Analysis, then Programming, then Design
mcq.stem: Object-Oriented Development has three phases. Which order and description is correct?

questions.tip: Mapping: Analysis = problem, Design = potential solution, Programming = actual software.

questions.q: Give four reasons why we use the object-oriented approach.
questions.a:
1. There are obvious mappings between real-world entities and system objects.
2. Easier maintenance.
3. Objects may be understood as stand-alone entities.
4. Objects are reusable components.

options: Obvious mapping between real-world entities and system objects; easier maintenance; objects are stand-alone entities; objects are reusable components
Faster execution; smaller binaries; no need for testing; no need for documentation
It removes all dependencies between components and guarantees thread safety
It eliminates the need for design and makes code self-documenting

questions.tip: The 'real-world mapping' reason is the one markers look for first.

questions.q: What is an object in the real world? Give two examples of attributes and two examples of behaviours for a customer.
questions.a:
An object is a thing, an entity - practically anything you can imagine that has its own identity, combining data and behaviour. Examples: a person, employee, account, transaction.
All objects have attributes, e.g. a customer has a name, address, gender.
All objects have behaviours, e.g. perform transaction, credit money, debit money.

options: It is a thing or entity with its own identity, combining data (attributes) and behaviour
It is a procedure that operates on data passed in from outside
It is a database row that stores only data, with no behaviour
It is a UML-only notation with no code equivalent
mcq.stem: Which statement about a real-world object is correct?

questions.tip: Key phrase: 'its own identity combining data and behavior'.

questions.q: In code, what are the following referred to as: (a) the name of an object, (b) its attributes, (c) its behaviour, (d) methods that describe how one class works with other classes?
questions.a:
(a) name -> type
(b) attributes -> properties
(c) behaviour -> method
(d) methods that describe how one class works with other classes -> interfaces

options: type, properties, method, interfaces
class, fields, function, abstract classes
variable, operations, event, packages
type, operations, property, namespaces
mcq.stem: In code, an object's name is a ___, its attributes are ___, its behaviour is a ___, and methods describing how one class works with others are ___.

questions.tip: Pure recall - one mark per term.

questions.q: Scenario: 'A university system allows a Student to enrol in Courses. A Lecturer teaches Courses. Each Course has a code, title and capacity.' Identify the candidate classes, the candidate operations, and the relationships.
questions.a:
Step 1 - identify nouns: Student, Course, Lecturer, Code, Title, Capacity.
Step 2 - identify verbs: enrol, teach.
Step 3 - candidate classes: Student, Course, Lecturer. Code, Title and Capacity are more likely to be attributes of Course.
Possible design: Student (studentId, name, Enroll()); Course (code, title, capacity, AddStudent()); Lecturer (lecturerId, name, Teach()).
Relationships: Student --enrols in-- Course; Lecturer --teaches-- Course.

options: Student, Course, Lecturer — Code, Title and Capacity are attributes of Course
Student, Course, Lecturer, Code, Title, Capacity — all six are classes
Student, Course, Enrolment, Teaching — Code, Title and Capacity are classes
University, Student, Course, Lecturer — all four are classes
mcq.stem: 'A university system allows a Student to enrol in Courses. A Lecturer teaches Courses. Each Course has a code, title and capacity.' What are the candidate classes?

questions.tip: Nouns -> candidate classes; verbs -> candidate operations. Not every noun is a class - some are attributes. Always say why.

questions.q: Is Object-Oriented Programming always the best approach? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No. Good software engineering chooses an appropriate approach. Procedural can be excellent for small, sequential or algorithmic tasks. Functional can be excellent for data transformation and processing. Logic can be excellent for rule-based reasoning. OOD is particularly useful for large systems with entities, relationships, responsibilities and changing state.

options: No — the approach should suit the problem: procedural for small algorithmic tasks, functional for data transformation, logic for rule-based reasoning, OO for large entity-rich systems
Yes — OOP is always best because it supports reuse and inheritance
No — procedural programming is always preferable for business systems
Yes — OOP is mandatory for any system with more than one class

questions.tip: Start with a clear 'No', then give one line per alternative approach.

questions.q: Why do we need Object-Oriented Design? Relate your answer to software complexity.
questions.a: Large systems contain many entities, rules, states and interactions. Changes in one part can unintentionally affect another part. Developers need clear boundaries and responsibilities. OOD provides ways to structure software so complexity can be managed. Goal: software that is understandable, maintainable and extensible. As a system grows from small to more features to more dependencies, OOP is one strategy for controlling complexity - it encourages assigning clear responsibilities, hiding internal details behind a public interface, and supporting reuse and extension through well-defined relationships.

options: Large systems have many entities, rules, states and interactions; changes in one part can affect another; OOD structures the software so complexity can be managed
Because procedural code cannot be compiled on modern hardware
To make programs run faster and use less memory
Because databases require object models to store data
mcq.stem: Why do we need Object-Oriented Design? Relate it to software complexity.

questions.tip: Use the growth story: small system -> more features -> more dependencies.

questions.q: Compare the procedural and object-oriented ways of solving the same enrolment problem, and state the real design question.
questions.a:
Procedural: student_name = "Ali"; course_code = "IT3001"; enrol(student_name, course_code) - data is held outside and passed into a function that updates shared structures.
Object-oriented: student = new Student("Ali"); course = new Course("IT3001"); student.enrol(course) - the Student owns the responsibility for requesting enrolment.
The syntax is not the main point. The design question is: WHO should be responsible for WHAT?

options: WHO should be responsible for WHAT
Which syntax is faster at runtime
Whether to use a class or a struct
How many parameters a method should take
mcq.stem: Comparing enrol(student_name, course_code) with student.enrol(course), what is the real design question?

questions.tip: The exam-ready sentence is the last one - 'WHO should be responsible for WHAT?'
